In summary, our research is concerned with

how children learn the syntax of their language, how they learn to use the language they have learned, how their language changes as they grow, and the relation between their language and other aspects of their development.
how people learn to speak a language, how they learn to understand what other people are saying, and how they learn to write.
the acquisition and maintenance of verbal behavior, with an emphasis on the acquisition of language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Skinner's Verbal behavior (1957) and its treatment of the acquisition of grammar and syntax, is not only adequate but superior to Chomsky's position.
the mentalistic approach has been a dead end and that the behavioristic approach is alive and well.
the behaviorist theory is not only adequate, but also superior to the mentalist theory in the explanation of the acquisition and use of language.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to account for all aspects of language acquisition in terms of operant conditioning, without the necessity of postulating any mentalistic constructs.

the behavior of the speaker can be explained in terms of the consequences of his own verbal behavior, the consequences of the verbal behavior of the speaker, and the consequences of the behavior of others.
we are able to explain the acquisition of grammar and syntax without the need of mentalist concepts, such as innate grammatical rules, mental representations, and the like.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the learning of grammaticality is not an insurmountable problem.
a behavior-analytical approach to language is viable and that the learning of syntax and grammar is no exception.
the learning of grammars and syntax can be understood as a special case of the learning of verbal behavior.
